c.tagline: Brazil's bar capital, where boteco culture meets Niemeyer's curves.

taxi.fareNote: Licensed taxis are white with a red BH crest; fares are metered (bandeira 1 by day, bandeira 2 at night/Sundays). Ride-hailing apps like Uber and 99 are widely used and usually cheaper.

emergency.note: 190 reaches the Military Police, 192 the SAMU ambulance service, and 193 the fire brigade; there is no single 911-style unified number.

solo.f: generally fine; extra caution at night

avoid.reason: Caution in the Hipercentro (downtown) at night

hood_desc: Belo Horizonte's buzzing social heart, packed with sidewalk botecos, craft-beer bars, restaurants and boutiques; the go-to base for nightlife and dining within easy walking distance.

An elegant, upscale and relatively calm residential district next to Savassi, known for chic wine bars, fine dining and the city's most luxurious hotel; suits travelers wanting sophistication and quiet close to the action.

The historic downtown core around Praça Sete and the Mercado Central, with the widest budget-hotel choice and the best public-transport links, including the metro; ideal for a convenient, no-frills base.
A leafy, charming and slightly quieter neighborhood between Savassi and the cultural Praça da Liberdade circuit, offering good-value hotels a short walk from the main dining and museum districts.

The green lakeside district in the north built around Pampulha Lagoon and Oscar Niemeyer's modernist architecture complex; a spread-out, scenic area good for a short stay or an early flight from nearby airports.
lodging: Ibis Budget BH Afonso Pena Savassi
Ouro Minas Hotel Belo Horizonte (Dolce by Wyndham)

water.note: Tap water is treated, but most locals and visitors drink filtered or bottled.

transit.hours: The metro runs roughly 5:15am to 11:00pm and buses from around 5:00am to midnight; MOVE trunk corridors run frequently through the day, with sparse late-night service filled by taxis and ride apps.
transit.note: The metro is a single line of limited tourist use; most travelers rely on the MOVE BRT, municipal buses, and ride-hailing apps to get around this hilly, spread-out city.
transit.pay: Pay bus and MOVE fares in cash or with the rechargeable Cartão BHBUS/Ótimo; the single Metrô BH line uses its own tokens/cards at station turnstiles. A metro ride costs about R$6 and a city bus about R$6 (each roughly $1.10), with discounted bus-to-bus transfers via the smartcard.

bus: Terminal Rodoviário de Belo Horizonte (Rodoviária, Praça Rio Branco)
train: Vitória-Minas Railway passenger train (EFVM) to Vitória from Estação Central

Taxi or ride-hail to central neighborhoods ~45-60 min

tip.r: A 10% service charge (serviço) is usually added to restaurant bills and is customary to pay; additional tipping is appreciated but not expected.

landmarks: Igreja de São Francisco de Assis (Pampulha)
Oscar Niemeyer's revolutionary curved-concrete church adorned with Cândido Portinari's azulejo tile murals, a UNESCO World Heritage masterpiece of modernist architecture.
Lagoa da Pampulha
A picturesque artificial lake ringed by Niemeyer's modernist buildings, offering some of the city's most iconic sunset photo opportunities.
Estádio Mineirão
One of Brazil's largest and most storied football stadiums, a pilgrimage site for soccer fans and host of major World Cup matches.
Praça da Liberdade
A grand tree-lined square surrounded by elegant early-20th-century palaces and cultural centers, serving as the city's civic and cultural heart.
Mercado Central (Central Market)
A bustling, colorful market beloved for its cheese bread, cachaça stalls, and lively atmosphere representative of Minas Gerais culture.
Palácio das Artes
A major cultural center and theater complex showcasing regional art, craft, and performances in the heart of downtown.
Serra do Curral
A dramatic mountain ridge forming the city's natural backdrop, prized by hikers and photographers for panoramic skyline views.
Museu de Artes e Ofícios
Housed in the beautifully restored old Central Station, this museum celebrates Brazilian craftsmanship and labor history in a striking historic setting.
Parque Municipal Américo Renné Giannetti
The city's oldest and most beloved park, a lush green oasis with lakes, gardens, and century-old trees in the urban core.
Casa do Baile
Another Niemeyer gem on Pampulha's lakeshore, this sinuous pavilion with its free-form canopy is a favorite subject for architecture photographers.

train.note: Brazil has almost no intercity passenger rail, but Belo Horizonte is a rare exception: Vale's Vitória-Minas passenger train runs daily from the Estação Central along the ore line east to Governador Valadares and Vitória on the coast, taking about 13 hours. It is slow, cheap and genuinely scenic. There are no international trains anywhere in Brazil.

bus.note: No international coaches. The Rodoviária beside Praça Rio Branco is central, with Cometa, Util and Gontijo running to Rio de Janeiro (about 6 hours), São Paulo (8) and Brasília (10); book through ClickBus (https://www.clickbus.com.br/) or Buser (https://www.buser.com.br/). Frequent buses also serve Ouro Preto and the colonial towns, about two hours away.

ferry.note: Belo Horizonte is inland in the Minas Gerais highlands with no navigable water, so there are no ferries.

half.name: Inhotim
half.blurb: An open-air contemporary art museum and botanical garden south of the city, pairing large-scale installations with tropical gardens.

full.name: Ouro Preto
full.blurb: A former gold-mining capital in the mountains, its steep cobbled streets lined with Baroque churches decorated by the sculptor Aleijadinho.

full.name: Congonhas
full.blurb: A pilgrimage town whose hilltop sanctuary is fronted by twelve soapstone prophet statues carved by Aleijadinho.
